newsitem.title: USA: MCI net hurt by competition, local investments.
newsitem.headline: MCI net hurt by competition, local investments.

text.p: Long-distance carrier MCI Communications Corp. said Wednesday its profits edged lower in the second quarter, hurt by competition in its core long-distance business and heavy spending to enter local markets.
MCI, based in Washington, reported second-quarter net income of $280 million, or 40 cents a share, down nearly 7 percent from $300 million, or 43 cents a share, a year ago.

The results, which were in line with a statement the company issued earlier this month regarding its second-quarter performance, matched Wall Street analysts' average estimate of 40 cents a share, according to research firm First Call.
However, investments in new ventures and markets reduced second-quarter earnings by $116 million, or 16 cents a share, the company said.
Total revenues rose to $4.8 billion in the second quarter, up 6 percent from the year-ago level of $4.6 billion.

Revenue from MCI's long-distance business reached $4.4 billion, an increase of $195 million, or 4.7 percent, over the second quarter of 1996 compared with the 12.7 percent growth rate MCI posted in the second quarter of 1996.

Long-distance revenue growth was the slowest in MCI's history, but reflected a general slowing among top long-distance carriers as they focus increasing resources on local service or wireless phone markets, analysts said.
MCI said its plan to target "higher-spending customers," coupled with strong competitive pressures, cut into revenues in the long-distance sector.

In the mass-market segment, the company's flagship consumer service, MCI One, rose 50 percent in the last three months, to reach 3 million customers. MCI said 85 percent of new MCI One sales came from non-MCI customers.

MCI's local phone service posted revenues of $80 million, up 82 percent from the second quarter of 1996, but the company said continuing regulatory hurdles to entering U.S. local phone markets hindered growth.

Earlier this month, MCI said anti-competitive practices by local phone companies would result in losses of $800 million in its local business -- double previous estimates -- with the potential for even greater losses in 1998.

MCI has begun offering local phone service in 25 U.S. metropolitan regions to date, having launched service in New Jersey only last week. It has said it plans to offer service in at least 31 U.S. local markets by the end of 1997.

MCI has said its local efforts have been impeded by Baby Bell operators who have stalled the opening of local markets to competition and by the slow pace of phone deregulation since the passage of the Telecommunications Act of 1996.

Despite the drain on earnings in 1997 and 1998, Chief Financial Officer Doug Maine said Wednesday that MCI remained committed to making hefty investments to enter U.S. local phone markets despite the expected impact on earnings.
"MCI will be among the first long-distance carriers to offer local service nationally," Maine said. "Now is exactly the time to make our move into local."
The increased losses from local market investments has cast a pall over its plans to merge with British Telecommunications Plc in a deal worth $21 billion.

British Telecom has said that terms of the merger may need to be renegotiated in light of the drain such investments will have on the merged company's results. The two companies are conducting a joint review of MCI local operations that is expected to be completed in the coming weeks, Maine said.
The proposed union, the largest trans-Atlantic merger ever, is under review by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission.

On Monday, FCC Chairman Reed Hundt endorsed the merger plan after the companies made assurances to regulators that British Telecommunications would provide equal access to other companies on trans-Atlantic phone networks and in Britain.
MCI's stock fell 50 cents to $35.25 on Nasdaq.
